chapter_theme: The Vidyadhara king gives the youth his daughter at an open gathering of kings, after which the youth gains the wheel and nine treasures through Indra's grace, subdues the Vidyadhara lords, returns with his queens to his father's city, installs a son and is sent off by his father to Indra's city.

283.reading: The king takes in the sage's word, weighs it, and sends word to the young man that he has seen him and that he should come.
283.nuance: Lines 3 and 4 do not say who is addressed or who carries the message; the reading takes it as the summons to the groom the sage had foretold.
283.event: The king, having heard the sage, sends word summoning the youth.

284.reading: The youth goes, taking his merit as his only wealth, meets the king face to face, and arrives gladly with the king's attendants.
284.nuance: Line 1 puts the youth's journey in terms of merit (புண்ணியன்), the same quality that later verses give as the cause of his rise.
284.event: The youth goes to the king, who receives him with joy and attendants.

285.reading: The king, glad, speaks sweet words of the youth, who is like Kaman without his sugarcane bow and has every fine mark, and then asks his ministers for counsel.
285.event: The king praises the youth and consults his ministers about giving him his daughter.

286.reading: The ministers, glad, warn that giving the bride to him alone would bring the other kings in anger, and so they send out word to the gathered kin and kings.
286.nuance: Line 4 is hard to parse; the reading takes the sending out of word as summoning the kings so the match is not a private one.
286.event: The ministers advise an open gathering of kings, and word is sent.

claims.claim: a bride given privately to one suitor brings the anger of the rival kings, so the choice is made public

287.reading: With the kings gathered, the swan-gaited bride, like nectar, deftly lifts a garland bright as lightning and puts it on the young man named earlier.
287.nuance: The bride chooses; the garland is hers to give, in front of the kings the ministers wanted present.
287.event: At the gathering of kings the bride garlands the youth.

288.reading: The king's grand sacrificial fire sets the wedding, and the pair delight in each other, while Manasavegan's mind is said to be afraid.
288.nuance: Line 4 breaks off in a hanging phrase about Manasavegan's mind, which verse 289 does not finish, so what he fears is left unstated.
288.event: The wedding is held at the fire and the couple unite.

289.reading: The hero mounts a swift elephant and appears in the middle of the long city of the Nagas, and the young women drink him in with their lotus eyes as though he were Kaman.
289.nuance: 'நாக நீள்புரம்' could be a city of Nagas or a serpent-named place; the Tamil does not settle which, and the closing 'நாள்' hangs into verse 290.
289.event: The hero rides the elephant into the city and the women gaze at him.

290.reading: The lord, who has set his mind on ruling by the wheel, goes to the mountain of the Vama Nagas, where those who see him are shown the wheel and the nine treasures.
290.nuance: The line ends in a list (the wheel, then nine treasures), and who gives them is not stated until the next verse names Indra's grace.
290.event: The hero goes to the Nagas' mountain, where the wheel and the nine treasures are seen.

291.reading: By Indra's gracious word the treasures are given to Kaman, and the garlanded beings of the mountain bow before him, in a number the verse gives obscurely.
291.nuance: Line 4, 'தோமினால் இரண்டொன்ற ஆயிரம்', is a hard count (two joined to a thousand?) and I do not fix it. Here Kaman, as in the other verses, is the hero's byname.
291.event: Indra's grace gives the treasures, and the mountain's beings bow to the hero.

292.reading: The wheel circles to the right and bows, and the greatly meritorious hero returns and at once brings every able Vidyadhara lord under his feet.
292.nuance: The Tamil names him a man of great merit (புண்ணியன்) in the sentence that tells the conquest, and so makes the victory a result of merit, not only of the wheel.
292.event: The hero, with the wheel, subdues the Vidyadhara lords in an instant.

claims.claim: the hero's power over rivals is the fruit of his merit

293.reading: Having won the Vidyadhara lords' tribute, he casts wealth to those who seek refuge and goes with the greatness of Indra to a city of unfailing mansions.
293.nuance: The verse joins conquest and giving: he accepts submission and then gives to those who take refuge.
293.event: The hero wins the Vidyadharas' tribute, shelters those who beg refuge and goes to a splendid city.

294.reading: Madanamanjikai, glad of heart, Vegavati and Anangavilasai are named among his queens, with more than eight thousand ladies besides.
294.nuance: The verse has no verb; it lists the queens and carries into verse 295, where the enjoyment is stated.

295.reading: After enjoying the pleasures of the rite and gathering good merit, he sets up a single sovereignty that grows by the fruit of what he had done.
295.nuance: 'வேள்வி' may mean the wedding rite or a sacrifice, and I read it as the rite of marriage and kingship; the verse does not say which.
295.event: The hero founds his sole sovereignty after the sacrifice and the joys it brings.

claims.claim: gathered merit comes back as sovereignty and pleasure in a later stage of life

296.reading: With his queens, bowed to by the Vidyadharas, he leaves the cloud-ringed mountain and goes to his father, the refuge of the gods.
296.nuance: The verse calls the father a refuge of the gods (வானவர் தஞ்சம்), which sets the father above the son's new rank.
296.event: The hero and his queens leave the mountain and go to his father.

297.reading: The city is hung with flower garlands, festoons and flags, and the king in his flower garland goes out to meet him and looks on him with wonder.
297.event: The father, the king, decks the city and goes out to meet his son.

298.reading: The son bows to his father's and mother's feet, and the moon-faced queens come and bow to their husband's father and mother in the same way.
298.nuance: The queens' bow includes his father and his mother; it shows the son's rank is held beneath the household's old order.
298.event: The son and his queens bow to his parents.

299.reading: After joyous embraces they enter the house, and the lord with the wheel sits in great splendour and gladly calls his sons.
299.event: They embrace and enter the house, and the son calls his sons.

300.reading: The peerless wheel-lord sets up Gomukan, Padumai's son born of her great labour, in rule.
300.nuance: Lines 3 and 4 are loosely joined; the reading takes 'அரசு நாட்டினான்' as installing Gomukan, but whether as king or as heir is not clear.
300.event: The hero installs Gomukan, Padumai's son, as ruler.

301.reading: His father, out of unfailing love and thinking of the parting, sends him off in burning sorrow, and the lord goes as he must to Indra's city.
301.nuance: Line 2 is damaged ('றந்த தான்'), and I read the parting as the father's grief at letting him leave.
301.event: The father, grieving, lets his son go and he sets off to Indra's city.

302.reading: The prince goes to the god Indra, bows at the worship of the Lord, takes the jewelled chariot at Indra's leave, and returns to his own city to live in splendour.
302.nuance: 'வாமன் பூசை' (the worship of Vaman?) could name the deity worshipped or its rite; the Tamil does not say who he is.
302.event: The prince visits Indra, worships, rides a gem chariot home and settles in his city.

links.note: Manasavegan, who had seized the pair in verse 266, is the one whose mind is afraid at the wedding.
links.teaches: The rival who once held the hero captive now fears him, so the wedding shows the rivalry turning in the hero's favour.

links.note: The sage's saying that the groom will rule the earth with the wheel is met by the wheel and nine treasures.
links.teaches: The sage's prophecy is fulfilled step by step, so the reader sees how the promised wheel comes to him through Indra's grace.

links.note: The sage promised the silver mountain's realms under his feet; here the Vidyadhara lords are brought under them.
links.teaches: The promise of the sage's earlier words is kept in the same terms, which marks the conquest as foretold, not chance.

links.note: The epic makes merit's fruit a throne and pleasure in this life, where the couplet calls virtue the companion that stays when you die.
links.teaches: Merit gathered earlier is repaid here as sovereignty, so the couplet's 'companion' is shown paying out in the same life it began.

gains.a: the verse's merit gets a test against the Kural's claim that virtue's worth is what survives death, which the verse alone does not state
gains.b: the couplet gets a case in which virtue's reward comes while the doer lives, a limit it does not state

links.note: At the height of empire and eight thousand queens, the Naladiyar says kings on elephants under umbrellas are carried off like all others; the next kandam is a renunciation.
links.teaches: The peak of enjoyment is set right before the work's renunciation kandam, so the Naladiyar's warning is the story's own turning point.

gains.a: the list of queens gets the Naladiyar's warning of what such splendour is worth, which the verse never voices
gains.b: the quatrain gets a case of a king's splendour at its height, which gives its warning a particular king to fall on

source_issues: Verse 288 line 4 breaks off in a hanging phrase about Manasavegan's mind.
Verse 289: whether 'நாக நீள்புரம்' is a city of Nagas or a serpent-named city is not settled.
Verse 291 line 4: the count 'இரண்டொன்ற ஆயிரம்' is obscure.
Verse 294 has no finite verb and runs into 295.
Verse 301 line 2 reads 'றந்த தான்', which looks damaged.
Verse 302 line 2: 'வாமன்' is not clearly the worshipped deity or its rite.
The Vidyadhara king's name, Neelavegan, comes from verse 278 of the earlier chapter; verses 283-302 call him only 'the king'.

cast.role: Udayanan's son, called the youth (காளை) and the lord of the wheel; a name not written in these verses
the Vidyadhara king whose daughter weds the youth; named in verse 278 of the earlier chapter, here called only the king
the ministers of the Vidyadhara king
the king's daughter who garlands the youth (Nagadattai in verse 278, unnamed here)
the young women of the city who gaze at the hero
Indra, who gives the treasures and the chariot
the garlanded beings of the mountain who bow to the hero
the hero's queens, among them Madanamanjikai, Vegavati and Anangavilasai
the king of Vatsa, here the father (வேலரசன்)
